newsitem.title: UK: EU pact offers little short-term cheer for the mark.
newsitem.headline: EU pact offers little short-term cheer for the mark.

text.p: The mark found its feet on Monday after sliding on the unveiling of the European Union's budget stability pact, but analysts saw little in the accord to restore it to health.
The pact approved strict budget deficit limits for members of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), but allowed for a political judgement on whether to fine those who overspend.

"The very fact we reach a stability agreement of any kind is mark-negative...simply because it keeps the momentum behind EMU relatively strong," said Joe Prendergast, currency strategist at Merrill Lynch.
The mark ended Friday's European session almost seven Italian lire down on the day at 984.50 lire after news agreement had been reached. It stood at 984.80 at midsession on Monday.

The post-EMU budget pact stipulates that a country overshooting the three percent budget deficit-to-GDP limit laid down in the Maastricht treaty on monetary union will avoid sanctions if its economy shrinks by two percent or more.

The agreement, reached at the Dublin summit after long, hard wrangling, partly satisfied German demands for automatic fines, while enshrining the element of political discretion that France was so keen to see, analysts said.

"The market is clearly responding to the impression that Germany, for all its tough talking, has once again compromised rather than risk derailing EMU," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Though the bulk of knee-jerk mark losses were probably seen on Friday, there is room for more mild softenening in the near term, analysts said.

But farther out, the implications for the currency market of the stability and growth pact -- as it was formally christened in Dublin -- are less clear, offering a glimmer of hope for the lacklustre mark.
Deutsche's Meggyesi said the accord enhanced the prospects of fiscal and price stability in the zone covering the "euro" single currency.
"This is encouraging for the euro's longer term stability prospects, and to this extent the pact cannot be seen as a negative development for the mark," he argued.

The euro could, however, be more prone to cyclical weakness than the mark as governments will be less able to use fiscal policy for anti-cyclical purposes. The burden on monetary policy will thus increase, resulting in lower interest rates, he said.
Some questioned the market's instinctive reaction to the pact, which was to bet on convergence between EU economies by selling the mark against its satellite European currencies.
The mark sank to a low of 3.3714 French francs late on Friday, coming within a whisker of slumping through 3.3710 three-and-a-half year low.

"The stability pact is not as soft as at first perceived as a degree of automaticity is included in the agreement which should still serve to make sustained convergence by the southern European states difficult," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank.
"Qualification for EMU will therefore still be dependent on GDP growth in 1997 which remains uncertain."
